utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. For the record, all the accused are here. Some of them talking. Defence teams are all here except for Mr. Josse, the Gvero Defence team, I suppose he's working elsewhere, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, Mr. Josse is working in the office today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that, thank you. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Nicholls. The witness is also present. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Bircakovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome once more. This afternoon, we will continue with the remaining cross-examinations. Then maybe there will be a re-examination, any possible questions from the Bench and you're free to go. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you continue, just for the record, Mr. Bircakovic, you'll recall having made the solemn declaration when you first started giving evidence. That is still valid, continues to be valid throughout your entire testimony. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you remember, we left it off with an exhibit, P00220. This is the diary of the duty officer of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade. Could we please look at the entries made on the 14th of July 1995, which is ERN number 00663926? In B/C/S this is on page 17, on e-court and page 14 of the English version. Sir, I suppose you have a clearer picture now. This is a logbook of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade. On the 14th of July 1995, an entry was made to the effect that the military police of the Bratunac Brigade was engaged in escorting Muslim refugees. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you did not have an occasion to see this document before?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After having looked at the document, would it mean anything to you if I told you that members of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade did indeed escort the convoy on the way to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at Exhibit number 3D133? This is an indictment issued by the Prosecutor's Office of Bosnia and Herzegovina against four members of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade. Can we please look at the pages 4 in both English and B/C/S version of this indictment? The same page in B/C/S version, please. There is something on the page that we wanted the witness to have a look at. Thank you. Mr. Bircakovic, could you please look at the bullet points 6 and 7 of this indictment relative to two -- four members of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade who are charged with providing security to the transport of detained Bosniaks from Bratunac on the 14th of July 1995. They served as guards, they controlled and provided security for the school gym and the complex of the schoolyard. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After having looked at this document, would you allow for the possibility that the convoy was indeed escorted by members of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How many of them do you think were escorting the convoy?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In -- according to your best knowledge, after having looked at the two documents, would you still consider that the convoy was escorted by the civilian police rather than the military police?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that there were also military policemen but it is also possible that there were civilian policemen there as well. Maybe they were both there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You're not sure, even after having looked at the two documents?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at what you did on the 13th of July? On the 13th of July, when did you return in the afternoon hours to the Standard barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that this was before 9.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, possibly before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You spent that night at home?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind what you've told us about the time, would you allow for a possibility that one convoy with prisoners arrived in Orahovac on the 13th of July, in the late evening hours? Is there such a possibility in your view?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I wouldn't know. I'm not aware of any such thing. I don't know. I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you allow for a possibility that that convoy, according to the information that you might receive subsequently, was escorted by the military police of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear from anybody, any of the men that you mentioned as having seen them on the 14th of July in Orahovac, did any of them tell you that they had arrived there on the 13th of July and that they had spent the entire night there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at another exhibit, a Prosecutor's exhibit, number P009 -- 296. This is something that we've already seen. This is a travel order for the Opel Rekord vehicle. P00296, for the record. Can we please look at page 2, both in the English and in the Croatian versions? Can we have the English version displayed at the same time, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We noticed that there are -- there is a discrepancy between the two versions. While we are waiting for the English version, sir, can you please look at the entries for 12th of July? It says Standard, Kajici, Standard. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of July according to this travel order, you went to Kajici. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. But this is what it says in the travel order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us where is Kajici?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think -- if this is in Kravica, then it is possible that Drago Nikolic may have been taken there, (expurgé) (expurgé) (expurgé) (expurgé)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let's go just out of an abundance of caution to private session for a brief moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since we have completely different information as to what kind of movement it was to Kajici village and that it had nothing whatsoever to do with Mr. Drago Nikolic, I want to ask you this: Is it possible that you drove on that day the assistant chief of staff for intelligence to Kajici village?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you have to explain to me where that village is because that name, Kajici doesn't tell me much. Where is it exactly, so I can know?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, then let me ask you this, and then I won't insist any more. Did you, while serving as a driver, have occasion to also drive assistant chief of staff for intelligence in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. You have to understand that I served as a driver to anyone who needed a lift and didn't have a car. If there was no other car available and I was free, that meant --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going to ask you about that date again but let me take you back once again to the 14th of July. You say you have no knowledge whatsoever about the arrival of the convoy on the 13th. Do you allow the possibility that on 14 July, in the morning, or, rather, before noon, another convoy carrying prisoners arrived at Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know only about that one convoy that we met and escorted to Orahovac. I don't know about any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of July, you were in Orahovac from 10.00 or 11.00 until the evening when you headed for the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, something like that. We also went to Zvornik and Karakaj. I wasn't there all the time but...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: From your colleagues, members of the military police of the Zvornik Brigade, did you hear at any point that on that day, on the morning of the 14th of July, a group of 20 to 30 soldiers arrived at Orahovac to replace the military policemen of the Zvornik Brigade who had spent the night of the 13th there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you again: To the best of your knowledge, are you telling us and is it your testimony that you know about the arrival of only one convoy over those two days, the 13th and the 14th of July, in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that one. I don't know about any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you would allow me, I would like to consult my client for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, just one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bircakovic, just one more question, or rather a suggestion. Is it possible, or rather, do you think I would be right in saying that on that day, the 14th, your vehicle drove ahead of the trucks rather than you being on the bus escorting it to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am 1 -- 1.000 per cent, no. I was there on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Madam Fauveau, I understand no -- still no further -- no cross-examination. The Gvero Defence team equally, no cross-examination? That leaves you, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a question about it might be correct the transcript it looks a bit inconsistent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 9, 3. "Your vehicle drove ahead of the trucks rather than you being on the bus." And I wonder if those are both supposed to be either bus or truck. Or maybe it's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it can be put straight to the witness. Witness, I'm going to read what you according to the transcript, said. Or, sorry, I'm going to read the question that Mr. Stojanovic read out or stated or put to you. And Mr. Stojanovic, please confirm whether this correct or not. Now it's getting complicated because we also have French interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as I can see, on the record, when I said ahead of the buses, it says ahead of the trucks. My question was whether he was driving before the buses, not trucks. I think I received his answer, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but his answer was, yes, I was on the bus. And what Mr. Nicholls raised is whether it should be bus or whether it should be truck. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. I was just asking about the question, the transcript, because I thought it was intended to be, I thought what Mr. Stojanovic said was did you drive ahead of the bus, not truck, so I think it's okay. I just wanted to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So let's proceed now, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Bircakovic, good afternoon. I have about 15 or 20 minutes worth of questions for you and so that you understand, I ask those questions on behalf of Vinko Pandurevic and I'll start by asking you whether he was somebody you were familiar with during your time in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, most of the questions you've been asked up until now have been about a few days in the middle of July of 1995. I want to ask you about August and September of 1995, when I think you were involved in combat in the region of the Krajina. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we went there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And would it be right that you went there with a unit of about 200 men that left from the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And would it also be right that the march from Zvornik to the Krajina took about a day?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the region of the Krajina which you went to was Drvar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, somewhere in between, not quite Drvar, a way before Drvar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'll mention a couple of other towns to you or villages, Grahovo or Glamoc, are they familiar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the unit that you went with remained in the Krajina, in those regions, for about six weeks, until the middle of September, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't go with that unit. I went with another unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you remember the dates when you were with the unit in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we stayed in Krajina for about seven days but not more than ten. I think we were replacing one of our units in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, do you remember whether the unit you were with was under the command of Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the unit was in that chain of command, but I know I was with Drago Nikolic, whom I drove there. Who was the main man, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. You were asked some questions yesterday by Mr. Bourgon about your knowledge of areas where bodies were dug up and reburied. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you discover at some stage that areas in, particularly, Orahovac had been excavated and bodies had been dug up and reburied elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people talked and that's how I learned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And didn't you discover when that had taken place?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'll put it to you. Didn't you discover that it had happened while you had been on combat in the region of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think maybe he can ask it a different way but I don't think it's fair to phrase it that way when he just said that he did not discover the time. So I don't think it's now -- I'm not being articulate. It's not fair to say he discovered it during this time when the witness has just said that he did not learn that particular time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in his previous answer, in response to the question, did you discover at some stage, by Mr. Haynes, he explicitly said, "People talked and that's how I learned." I don't see much difference between learned and discovered, if it is in the context that it has been said. I mean, to me, learned means here found out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand. My point was the question was: Didn't you discover when that had taken place? No. Didn't you discover that it had happened while you had been on combat. Maybe I misheard the question but I thought...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, but I still think that if the question is, didn't you discover that, to me it's equivalent to didn't you learn about that at the same time. Anyway, I don't know if you agree with Mr. Nicholls or not, Mr. Haynes, but if you think it needs or should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm simply trying to avoid calling up pages of his interview into e-court. This is something he said to the investigator and I'm putting it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Proceed. Let's proceed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Bircakovic, it's right, isn't it, that you found out that bodies had been dug up and reburied at Orahovac during the period that you had been on combat in the Krajina? Didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that upon my return, but when they did the digging and how it happened, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I want just to see whether we can -- I can jog your memory as to when you did return, and I'd like, please, if we could see in e-court 7D486, and it's the second page of that document. Now, Mr. Bircakovic, I'm going to have to ask you to help us here because this document is only in Serbian, so if you can, I want you to read it for us. I'll tell you the bit you've got to read. But can we start by looking at the date? We can see there it's the 17th of September and above that at the top of the page, do you agree that says the 16th of September of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I'd like you to read for us, if you can, we can make it a little bigger if it would help, the second paragraph there, just under the first line. Do you see? It contains the word "11.30". Would you read that out for us, please?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot make it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, with your leave, Mr. President, I'll ask Mr. Sarapa to read it out and see whether the witness agrees with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Today at 11.30, the 2nd DB returned to Zvornik led by Lieutenant-Colonel Commander Vinko Pandurevic from the area of responsibility of the 2nd KK." I suppose it's Krajina Corps. And DB means Drina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sarapa. Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would it be right that you returned to Zvornik with your unit on the 16th of September of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There were two trips, two departures. I think the one when Vinko Pandurevic went is not the same one as we accompanied the convoy to that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That may be right but what I'm asking you is whether the 16th of September is right for the date when you came back, not when you left.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when the return was, but -- and I don't know how long that stint was. I know that one stint was 45 days and another was less than seven, when Krajina was falling and the troops were returning to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear about this, are you saying that there was one stint which you did that was 45 days?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I went to that front line for about five or six, maybe seven days. We didn't stay long at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, then, Mr. Bircakovic, I'll leave that alone. You mentioned very briefly when you were answering questions to Mr. Nicholls that between being a member of a tank platoon and being a military policeman, you had been in a unit known as the Drina Wolves. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that would have been in 1993 and 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe, yes, in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I think you were part of a platoon of 10 or 15 men; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Which was part of the whole unit which comprised 150 to 200 men; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many men there were. It was a unit but I don't know how many men it had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it was a unit that had some buildings which passed as barracks, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not have any buildings. There were just ordinary houses in which people lived, and our men were accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And where were those houses?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kiseljak. That's perhaps 13 to 15 kilometres from Zvornik towards Bijeljina, and maybe 200 or 300 metres off the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how far from Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one and a half, maybe two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you know the Vitinka bottle factory in Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How far were those houses from that building?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the same distance, a kilometre and a half, maybe two.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And as the crow flies, how far from the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe 1.5, 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, lastly, you reported to the chief of the military police, Miomir Jasikovac, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander then. I don't know what you mean. When?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, in 1995, from whom did you take your orders?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, company commander. He was that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you ever take orders from anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received orders -- well, what do I know? If I had to drive somebody, I did. I received orders from the duty operative officer, from Drago Nikolic, Trbic, Jasikovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on the 14th of July of 1995, to your knowledge, did Mr. Jasikovac receive any orders from the brigade commander or his deputy?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what about the chief of security, after you'd taken him to this meeting? Did it appear to you he was taking orders from the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. It was not a brigade meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, did it appear to you that he reported any orders or reported on any of his tasks to his brigade commander during the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether there were reports or not. I didn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What about on the 15th of July, when you went to some schools with Mr. Jasikovac? Did it appear to you that he was reporting to the brigade commander about what he was doing on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I was a driver. I didn't know what went on between commanders, what messages were conveyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bircakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Haynes. Is there re-examination, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you about one question from yesterday. This is at page 11132. You were asked: "And driving besides the water point, you did not stop. Those bodies were visible from the road, is that so?" And you said, "Well, yes." And I just want to make sure, because that was -- there were two questions in the question to you. One, you'd already testified that you saw the bodies. My question to you is before that, did the car stop? Did you stop either on the way to the IKM or back when you passed the field of corpses by the water point?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not stop. We went directly, I've already told you, it was dark and in the headlights you could see, on the left-hand side, going up there, that there were bodies but we never stopped, either on the way there or on the way back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you tell, driving by at night, whether any of those bodies might have been people still alive who needed help? Was that possible to see?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I mean, we couldn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Nothing else now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Witness, you testified to the fact that on the 14th of July you went to the forward command post to pick up Mr. Nikolic. When you were there that morning, did you see anyone else at the forward command post when you picked up Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I didn't find anybody there. This forward command post is on a hill-top, something like a prefabricated holiday home, and this is where the officer -- officers would stay if they were sent to that forward command post. As I went up there, as I arrived, he had already been informed that I was on my way, he was waiting for me in front of the house, on the road. He got into the car and we drove off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. And then when you went back to the forward command post in the evening to pick up his personal effects, I take it from your answer originally, your original testimony, that you didn't go in to the building at that time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: So again, you don't know if there was anyone else in the forward command post at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BIRCAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Prost. One moment, I need to confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bircakovic, it means that your testimony ends here. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony, and we also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's start with the documents that the Prosecution wishes to tender. You have circulated a list already.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. No modifications to the list, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I take it that all the Defence teams have got a copy of this list. Any objections from anyone of you? We hear no objections, so these documents are being admitted as exhibits and they will be given the corresponding number by our staff. Any of the Defence teams wishes to tender any documents? Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No documents, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Likewise, Mr. President, no documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We will not tender also any documents, although we submit one document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I'm asking you because I was just reading it actually. And I take it that there are no other Defence teams that wish to tender any documents? Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, could 7D486, the two pages from the diary of the duty operations officer be marked for identification pending translation, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from Prosecution or from any of the Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, not to Mr. Haynes' exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic? I see. All right. Okay. I thought you had an objection. All right. So this document, or two pages, thereof will be marked for identification pending translation. That concludes the testimony of Mr. Bircakovic. And we can move to the next witness, who is here for cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't exactly know what Mr. Zivanovic meant when he said we will not tender any documents although we submit one document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. He had given -- handed out a list indicating that it was his intention to tender parts of the witness's statement to the OTP and I understand that he's changed his mind and he's withdrawn -- that he will not be tendering. That's how I understood him. If I misunderstood you, Mr. Zivanovic, please correct me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Brunborg.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And pleased to welcome you back on behalf of the Trial Chamber. You're here for cross-examination. A long time has passed since you were here last so you need to make again your solemn undertaking to testify the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir, please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, I notice also the presence in the courtroom of the ex parte Defence expert, Nikolic Defence expert. Ms. Nikolic, could you introduce your expert or your expert herself introduces herself?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, we will introduce the lady. This is Professor Svetlana Radovanovic from the University of Belgrade who is our joint witness for four Defence teams in this case, Popovic, Beara, Nikolic and Pandurevic. She is an expert on demography.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And welcome, ma'am, welcome, Professor. Yes, I have on my list five of the Defence teams that wish to cross-examine this witness. The ones who will not be cross-examining him at least for the time being are the Gvero and Pandurevic teams. I have two of the others that have requested an hour and a half each. I suggest that either of you will start with the cross-examination, either the Beara or the Nikolic Defence teams, unless there is a different arrangement in place between you or amongst you. Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honours. This has been arranged and we will be the first to examine Mr. Brunborg, and I believe that we will be followed by the Beara Defence team. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Brunborg, I'm Jelena Nikolic. I'm Jelena Nikolic and I'll start the cross-examination today. First I would like to ask you, before I start talking about your CV and the papers that you have published so far, as well as the expert findings and the witness testimonies, when you were given the task to work on Srebrenica, how did you define Srebrenica? What was its territory? What did it encompass and what did your work involve when it came to Srebrenica as such?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I was asked by the team that was investigating Srebrenica to look at cases of people who had gone missing from Srebrenica in relation to the events when Srebrenica fell on the 11th of July 1995. And Srebrenica, as you know, can mean either the municipality or opstina, or the city or town of Srebrenica. So it was actually the town that fell, not the whole municipality, I believe, and the places people went then disappearing or were reported as disappearing from various places from Srebrenica itself, in the town itself or many other locations near the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you roughly remember what towns were involved in addition to Srebrenica and the municipality of Srebrenica? What other places were involved?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Especially Potocari, of course, because many people walked from Srebrenica to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you remember Han Pijesak maybe?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that name.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Vlasenica, Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What I would like to know is this: If you remember Bajina Basta, Ljubovija, Valjevo? Do you remember these names?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last ones, I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Those are three places in the territory of Serbia. Maybe I can jog your memory by reminding you that in your report dated 16 November 2005, you mentioned these three places as well. My question is this: Why did you deal with territories and places which were outside the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we based our work on family members who had reported their family members as missing, and the report, and the last place the person, the family member, had been seen alive. And in some cases, that was in Serbia and not in Bosnia. Serbia is not just a few kilometres away from Srebrenica, as you know. So this information comes from the family members of the victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you considered these municipalities relevant for your further studies?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would like to move on to another topic. I've read your CV. I know that you come from Norway, which is a well-regulated state, and where there is a well-regulated register of the population. I would like to ask you would you have any experience working on any censuses anywhere else in the world but in Norway?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On censuses, I worked on Botswana and Zambia in Africa, also I'm also familiar with the census of Albania, and Bosnia, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the censuses that you've mentioned, how important are they as a source of information about the population in the states where the censuses are carried out?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: For these countries, which lack good registers, the census is one of the most important sources of information about the population, especially its composition, with regard to age and sex and residence, where they live, and also with regard to factors like education and household composition.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How much do you know about the last census which was held in Bosnia in 1991? Did that census contain any other information, save for that that you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, it contained information on language spoken, on ethnicity, on religion, profession, very detailed information on where people lived, referring to enumeration area.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The 1991 census, did it also contain the personal identification number of the citizens? And I'm only referring to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct but not for everybody. For approximately two-thirds, or a little more than two-thirds of the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Was it in 1981 that the personal ID number was introduced in the former Yugoslavia? Are you familiar with that information? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any explanation as to how come that one-third of the population was not registered under their personal ID number when the census was carried out in 1991? Was it ever explained to you?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not do any field-work, of course, but I believe that many people did not know their number or did not have records available that could -- that they could use to report their unique number, the maticni broj.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. If I understand you well, we are talking about the 1991 census which was carried out by the state, and the citizens did not volunteer to come forward with the information about themselves. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were enumerators going around collecting information in the census. I do not recall whether the census was compulsory or not. I believe it was; there was a special census law. I believe it was compulsory but I don't remember the law. But also I believe that people were not penalised if they did not answer all the questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I have to come back to this ID number. That is something that is property of the state, of the police. It has to be reported to the census commission regardless of the willingness or ability of the population to provide that number to the enumerators. Do you know what I'm talking about? It's not up to the citizens to provide that number. That number can be obtained from the police where the citizens are registered under that number.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the Minister of Interior, the MUP, had a register with names, and with the identification number. But to transfer that to the census, I don't know how that is all physically possible, and I doubt that the statisticians conducting the census would allow that because this is -- a census is a statistical exercise. It is not done for administrative purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I won't go into any details of that. I'll move to something else. However, since we are talking about Bosnia in 1991, the census was carried out by the state, the personal data with the ID number can be found at the police, the population reports for the census with their ID cards containing all that, and my question is still: How do you account for the fact that one-third of the population does not appear in the 1991 census with their ID numbers? Have you ever received any explanation about that? They are supposed to report to the census with their ID cards and their ID cards were supposed to contain that information.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not received any information about that, but there are missing data on all variables so it's not surprising that the sort of technical, highly technical item like ID number was not reported. Although it's disappointing in a way that people did not report that more. I did, by the way, an analysis of the identity numbers because there is a check digit at the end of it which is a function of the previous numbers and to check whether they were correct or not, and I believe I found they were correct in most cases but also some were incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll go back to the task that you received in 1997, when you first started to work for the Office of the Prosecutor. At that time, you were faced with the way data were compiled and analysed for the persons that went missing in the course of the fall of Srebrenica and after the fall of Srebrenica in 1995; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for the date. I think I was tasked with this in 1998, not in 1997. I started to work here at the beginning -- the middle of 1997, and my first job was to find out what were the available data sources, what methodology should we use? And I quickly realised that the only safe methodology was to base my work on data on individuals. Individual data on victims, on pre-war population and on post-war population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's something not clear in my mind. You started by correcting Ms. Nikolic as regards the date, explaining that the reference to 1997 was wrong because you were tasked in 1998. But then the rest of your answer refers to the second half of 1997, and not to 1998. I mean, there may be a mistake in the transcript but perhaps you could explain. You have the transcript in front of you. I'm referring to lines 15 to 21 of page 27.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry for not being clear. My task when I started to work here was to investigate and estimate the number of -- the demographic impact of the armed conflicts in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in June 1997 when I started. Later this was narrowed down to studying Srebrenica so a first half year or so or more than that was spent on general issues. I did a lot of work on other areas of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And in 1998, you were then tasked with reference to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If I understand it well, the task that was given to you involved the period between 11 July 1995 and the end of 1995. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So you were about to complete the list of missing persons, missing men, for that period and to provide as precise an identification as possible?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. There were already some lists available on missing persons, and I was asked then to look very carefully at these lists, evaluate them, check their quality, combine them into one list, and which would be as good as possible, eliminate all doubtful cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You said that there existed possible lists of missing persons. I suppose that you mean the ICRC list that had been compiled already by that time?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. They started in early 1990s collecting data on missing persons for all of the former Yugoslavia and they published several lists for Bosnia. The -- they were using version 3 and version 4. I don't remember the exact dates now but the dates of those but those dates are in my report. I think the last version 4 was dated 1999, July 1999, I think. They later produced more lists and now it's continuously updated on a web site. So the report that is presented here is based on the most recent version available. Moreover, if I may, then there was a list of missing persons compiled by the Physicians for Human Rights, PHR. Also, two versions or so. And we combined all of these lists together, evaluating the quality, eliminating duplicates and overlaps in the records and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That means that when you began your work, you used those two sources, the ICRC list, for which family members reported missing persons, and the ante mortem base?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Apart from the ICRC lists, did you use original information from the questionnaire of the ICRC, where family members provided more details such as profession, occupation, whether somebody was a soldier or a civilian, and such things?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That information was not provided to us by ICRC. It was date of birth; sex; name; family name; father's name; place and dates of disappearance; perhaps place of birth or place of residence. I'm not quite sure about the last items.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you ask to get an insight into the questionnaires of the ICRC that served as a basis for the ICRC list on their web site? Did you use the raw information from those questionnaires or did you just use the data from the lists?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I've seen the questionnaire, an empty, blank questionnaire but as I told you just now, we did not get that other information. ICRC is very protective about the information they are releasing, to preserve the neutrality so they have access to all sides in a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But did you ask for such information, since you saw a blank questionnaire, and it contains a question whether the missing person is a military person or a civilian? Did you ask for that particular information in regard to every single person reported as missing?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We made general requests for information, and I believe it was denied, that we could only get the information that had already been provided in electronic format. For example, there was also on the questionnaire they asked about ethnicity, which was not provided to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In addition to the sources such as the PHR and ICRC, all your findings from 2000 onwards, that you shared with the public, apart from being based on these two sources, I understood that you controlled these two sources with references such as the census of 1991 in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You compared these two sources to the census data.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We compared the data with the census for several reasons. In some cases, to check whether two records that were almost identical or quite -- or quite identical, whether they represented different persons or the same person, and we also checked to see whether that these were real persons, the missing, the persons who had been reported as missing, that they were not made up, which were for political reasons, which was sometimes an accusation, and we found a very large overlap, I think 87 per cent, we found 87 per cent of those reported as missing, we found in the census and the remaining 13 per cent can be accounted for by lack of good enough information to perform the matching. All this was done electronically. We also did visual inspection in certain difficult cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So practically that 1991 census was a reference source for you, that provided a basis for your later findings?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. As you know, it was conducted right on the eve of the conflicts, on the 31st of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that for 30 per cent -- 13 per cent of persons, the data didn't match between the census and other sources. How did you present those 13 per cent in your later findings?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason why they did not match is in most cases because probably because of spelling errors in the census, lack of full date of birth and other particulars, that did not either in the list of missing persons or in the census, which did not allow for matching. So in a few cases we assume that we pro-rated the results with also additional 13 per cent but in most cases, this was not essential that we did not find those 13 per cent. Because we had already the list of missing persons, and when we found 87 per cent, that was a very good evidence that these are real and not fictitious persons, that they lived in Bosnia in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time it's convenient for you, Ms. Nikolic, we will have a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, just one more question before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So we can agree, sir, that those 13 per cent remained unidentified?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely, because they were identified in the list of missing persons, with name, dates of birth, name of father, family name, and so on. But they did not have, say, the identification number, the maticni broj was not recorded by the ICRC. At least we did not get it. So they are not unidentified but we did not succeed in matching all those with the census information. Also, they could have also been some people who moved to Bosnia after the census was taken, and reported as missing, say, coming from others of the republics. And also a census is not perfect, you should remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is a good time for a break, Your Honours. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, in spite of the redaction, we can live with 25 minutes, Madam Registrar? Yes, 25 minutes break, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, again, sir. Let me come back to the last answer you gave us before the break. When we discussed the 13 per cent of persons who were identified or, rather, reported to the ICRC list, as far as I understood from your findings so far, on one side you had the ICRC and PHR lists and on the other side you had the 1991 census in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that you qualified in your findings as a strong source of population data in Bosnia and Herzegovina and to establish that a person from the ICRC list indeed existed, you looked for that person on the list of the 1991 census, to establish that the person was then a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, almost correct. Not that the person was a citizen, just that the person was enumerated in Bosnia in 1991. Citizenship is not related to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Right. So we can agree that on that list there were also persons who were listed in the census in Bosnia-Herzegovina but were possibly working abroad, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the list of missing persons, you mean? In the census?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the census, yes.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are -- in demography or population statistics, there are two principles for census taking, it's the de facto and the de jure principle. And I think, as far as I remember, the Yugoslavian censuses was sort of a mixture but mostly de jure, so that in some cases, they did in fact include people who worked abroad temporarily but they were not supposed to include people who were permanently abroad, and of course, to include them somebody needed to report them so if a whole family went abroad for work or employment or other reasons then there was nobody to report them so I don't think there were that many who were enumerated, who did not live there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the census encompassed permanently residing people on the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, except for those who were temporarily working abroad, yes. Now, people are also enumerated who were just visitors but they were supposed to later to be transferred to the right place where they actually lived, if there was a visitor on census day they should not -- they might be enumerated but they should later be transferred to the proper place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the law on census from 1982 and 1991 for the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen the law but I don't remember the details of it now. It's almost ten years ago since I looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let me come back to those 13 per cent that we discussed before the break because I think that is the crucial point of our discussion. When you said that those were persons listed by the ICRC, would you agree with me that they were recorded and listed based on information that their family members provided about them?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, in 95 per cent of the cases, the victims were reported by family members.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And in order to establish that the person really existed and he or she was a resident of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you used that strong source, as you called it, the 1991 census in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to establish that, the existence of that person?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did sort of an overall electronic matching which resulted in the 87 per cent. In some cases we needed to discuss the particulars of a given person, then we did it visually and looked up the census, because then we -- it was much easier to overcome spelling mistakes in the writing of names and so on. To do a proper matching electronically the information has to fit, be exact, of course, unless we introduce certain fuzziness criteria, as we call them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the other sources you used in your work, apart from the two that we discussed and the PHR. Did you also consult electoral lists?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We consulted or we compared the list of missing persons with the electoral lists of 1997 and 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you consult later electoral lists from 2000 and 2006?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the first report, from the year 2000 we consulted the 1997 and 1998 voters lists and for the current report, the 2005 report, we also consulted, I believe, the 2005 voters lists. 2006, we could not consult because it happened after the report was written.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you attempt in your work to search for new sources?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, the record may reflect that in response to the last question the witness was referring to a document, and I think he was trying to confirm the answer of the previous question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that so, Mr. Brunborg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, now I checked table 2 in our report of the 16 of November 2005 where it's clear that we consulted the voters list 1997 and 1998, and the year 2000. And in response to your last question, yes, we did look for other sources. The other post war source that we used was the list of displaced persons collected by the UNHCR and the government of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: May I ask to you answer this question? When we line up all these sources, all of them have a certain motive behind them. Censuses are made by the state. The list of missing persons are based on family members' reports. Electoral lists are based on voluntary reporting of persons who are of age to vote. So all these sources provide relatively different data.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But since, as you said, the motive or the idea behind each of them varies, then in fact they support each other. These are -- some of them are administrative sources, I'm very familiar with the use of administrative data sources in my own country and the use of other sources collected for other purposes than those we are interested in now is -- can strongly support, because it eliminates, say, a bias, a certain ideological bias against the data source. For example, the census was not collected with the idea that they should be used to identify missing persons, so there is no bias in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just one thing, what about the methodology behind these sources? Was it identical?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. Thank you. The census was, as I said a state undertaking taken by enumerators going from house to house. A statistical exercise. The voters list was done to make a voters register to be used for elections. And it was conducted by the OSCE, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe. The ICRC missing list was collected to locate missing persons, missing family members and their fates and trying to reunite family members. The PHR list was collected, was an ante mortem database, as you said, to help in identifying exhumed bodies. And finally, the DDPP, the list of displaced persons was collected to aid displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this very exhaustive answer. Let me pick up on what you said. All these lists, all these sources, came into being in different periods; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The census was in 1991, the ICRC list was done in 1995, and we already discussed other sources. Is it possible in statistics to compare different periods looking at the same statistical data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. And here we are -- since we are based, we are basing our work on individual data on individuals, we do in fact have what we call longitudinal data for the same population or overlapping populations. This is often done; for example, a survey could be taken of the same population at many different times, say, one or two or three years apart and here we have in fact a longitudinal database. We have a snapshots of the population of Bosnia taken in 1991, 95, 1996, 1997 so on. Voters list 98, 2000 and so on. So there are different lists, for different purposes but covering the same population. But none of them is covering the entire population perfectly. The census is the closest but even there, that one has shortcomings. As time passes by, then more people are born that were not enumerated in the census, people move in, people die, and people move out.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, based on everything that you have told us about all this information and sources, to what extent did they all help you establish the number of people in Srebrenica in 1995, when you were doing your study?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most important part was of course the lists of missing persons established by ICRC. I said version 4 was from 1999. That was wrong, I checked, it was July 1998. We used version 3 for January 1997 and the 2005 version. And the PHR. And also for the present report, we looked -- we used data collected by the ICMP, the national commission for missing persons, based on exhumations so that's an additional data source that was not available when we started this work in 1998, 1999. And so we tried to combine the different data sources in imaginative ways to check the quality and the mostly we find very few inconsistencies. The data sources mostly support each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Are those all those sources that in your 2005 report quoted as the basis for assumption that there were about 40.000 people in Srebrenica, and were you able to establish their age and gender based on those sources?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That estimate of 40.000 people in Srebrenica before it fell has been reported by various organisations, but we do -- there is no list, no general count. It could -- it was collected for also for receiving rations. Maybe it was inflated; I don't know. But we have not used that number at all but what we have used is the census again. We matched the missing persons with those who were enumerated in Srebrenica especially and other municipalities in 1991. So we know how many of those who lived in Srebrenica in 1991 who were then -- who went missing in 1995. The very same persons. Finding very high proportions of all those who whether enumerated in 1991 who were reported as missing four years later.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, I don't know whether my conclusion would be correct, if we say that from the aspect of profession and sources, did not have the reliable data based on which you could establish the correct number of the population in Srebrenica on the eve of the conflicts that took place in 1995, would I be right in coming to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. What we only know for certain is the number who were enumerated in 1991 and as you know, there were many flows of people out of Srebrenica a few years before 1995 and there were flows into Srebrenica also from other municipalities and surrounding areas so we do not know. But the stories are that it was a large number of people there in early July 1995 and they were not allowed to escape. But that's correct. But the number of people, whether it was 20.000 or 40.000 is not really, as far as I can see, very significant when we discuss the number of people who are missing or dead after the fall of Srebrenica, because we have those lists of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as the sources are concerned, I have one more question. In your work, did you use the official statistical data which were compiled in 2004, for the period between 1992 and 1995, for the deaths that were established during that period, and these data contain information about both entities within the federation?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was done by my colleagues after I left. I'm not quite sure whether those data were used to check whether a person on the missing list was dead. I believe they were. Because on the list or the ICRC list of missing persons, then there are several thousands who have been found to be dead, and various sources were used for that, but the information came mostly from ICRC itself but also from other sources. So I'm sorry but I'm not quite sure about the details about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But you personally did not consult the Dem 2 database when you prepared your report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I know there were very few people in the official established database that were concerned with Srebrenica missing persons, because most of the -- those deaths in that report, in that official database concerned people from other areas of Bosnia and also people who died from natural causes, so only a small number of them relate to Srebrenica. As you also know, Srebrenica is in Republika Srpska, and this database was established by the federation, and at that time we did not yet have access to the -- I don't know if it has been established a similar database for Republika Srpska, which would then cover Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I believe that we are talking at cross purposes. I'm talking about the Dem 2 database that was commissioned by the Prosecutor's Office in 2004 containing the official data on the deaths between 1992 and 1995, both in the Republika Srpska and the federation. Judging by your answer, I believe that we are talking about two different things.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise for misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The database that I've just mentioned was not consulted by yourself, judging by your answer. You did not consult that particular database, the one commissioned by the Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: My colleagues did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll go back to your 16 November findings, 2005. On page 3, when you are talking about the context, I'm going to quote, I believe that you will find the same text in the English version, on page 3, unfortunately I can't show it to you on the e-court. This is what you say in paragraph 1 under the title "Context". Two penultimate sentences. "The total number of victims is not known. The exhumation that were carried out by the local Bosnian commissions for search for missing persons revealed over 7.000 bodies from a broadly defined territory of Srebrenica." We have had occasion to listen to the testimonies by an anthropologist and a pathologist and so far we have not heard this data, that 7.000 bodies have been discovered. Would you please tell me what source did you use to establish that fact in your report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's based on public information from the ICMP which has report that says that we have exhumed -- no, they have blood samples of the relatives of approximately 7.800 persons, and they have exhumed as of when this report was completed, in November 2005, approximately 2.600 bodies. No, they had exhumed more but they had identified 2.591 bodies, because there were many bodies that were awaiting identification. So -- hmm. The total number of bodies that had been exhumed in November 2005, I need to check the report to see what that number was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: There is no need for you to go into that trouble. I just -- this may be a misunderstanding on page 12 of your report, when you're talking about the data provided by the PIP institution and ICMP, a reference is made to 7.000 body-bags. Did you interpret this information incorrectly or were you dealing with two different pieces of information when you stated this?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 11?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Could you point out exactly where it is written? The number of missing persons from Srebrenica is 7.789. That was the number of persons that relatives had donated blood samples for. So that's one. So that is, in effect --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I believe that we are talking about one sentence before that. "According to the information of PIP, approximately 7.000 body-bags containing mortal remains are stored in various morgues in Tuzla." I apologise. This has entered the transcript but I will repeat. I believe that we are talking about one sentence before the one that you've just read out. It says, "According to the PIP data approximately 7 .000 body-bags containing mortal remains" --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I touched the wrong channel here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you assist him, Madam Usher, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't hear any translation. Which channel is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Number 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So if you could please repeat your question or comment?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Gladly. It is possible that there has been a mistake. I'm going to read to you the sentence before this one and the sentence reads: "According to the PIP data, approximately at least 7.000 body-bags containing mortal remains are stored in various morgues in Tuzla." But when we look at the sentence on page 3, where you're talking about 7.000 bodies, are we talking about two different pieces of information from two different sources or is that one and the same piece of information which has been treated differently on these two different pages of your report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: On which number on page 3 are you referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The one we mentioned a while ago. After the title, "Context".

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Paragraph -- chapter 2, actually, and the sentence is in the middle of the first paragraph, the one that I had read out to you when I put my previous question to you.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that is about the same. They have uncovered -- "ICMP has uncovered more than 7.000 bodies out of the broadly defined Srebrenica territory." And on page 11 it says 7.000 body-bags are stored in the Tuzla morgues. I think that is -- should cover the same, but as you know, a body-bag can contain -- the contents of a body-bag is not always clearly defined and bone samples can be found in different body-bags and several bone samples from the same person in one body-bag, et cetera. So DNA analysis and identification and comparison with victims has to be done before we can say for sure how many people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Correct. I agree with you. This is exactly what you have explained in your findings. The same organisation, ICMP, provides information that 7.780 missing persons, their relatives provided blood samples in order to establish their identity. Are you aware of the fact whether the blood sample donors were two or three members per person or, in other words, whether these blood donors had the identical number with regard to the number of missing persons or victims? In other words, was the number of donors the same for each and every victim?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Definitely not. It varied from one to three or four or even more, because the more family members you have, the higher is the probability that an analysis gives the right answer, the right result, especially if there are no close living relatives, say a sibling or parents or children, and you only have, say, data on cousins or grandparents, you need, I'm not an expert on this, but then you need more blood samples. So definitely you need -- the number of blood samples is much, much higher than the number of victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll go back to the sources that we've already discussed before the break, and the quality of the sources that you dealt with and also the problems that you faced when compiling your report. Would there be a list that would reflect the quality of data as to how many people were identified in your list, without any mistakes, where there was 100 per cent correct identification, with the identification of the 1991 census? In other words, is there 100 per cent match between the list of the missing persons and the ICRC list with the data in the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not quite understand your question. There will never -- there is no 100 per cent match here because there are errors in all lists, both the missing lists and the census list and I said that we managed to find 87 per cent. If we had done more work, spent even more time, the proportion would have been higher. It's exactly because the nature of the conflict and the difficult war situation that we do not -- we have inexact data and we have to rely on many different sources. In a peaceful truly functional, well-administered situation, the data will be much better but then we would not have this kind of the need for such data on the missing persons, ironically.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The data or the most relevant data I'm sure that you will agree with me is the date of birth, the date and month and year of birth of a certain person. Is that the most important data about a person?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that the name is the most important.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I agree. In addition to the name it would be the date of birth, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the name consists of three parts in the former Yugoslavia, first name, family name and also father's name, and many people have the same name, which sometimes caused confusion, but after that, date of birth, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have pre-empted my next question but I will go back to the date of birth. How many people on the list of missing persons from Srebrenica had a known date of birth?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need to consult, if you want an exact answer, it's in the report. Year of birth was missing for just a few persons, one or two or three people. Month was missing for more, and the date of the month was missing for a total for, I think, around 30 per cent, in that order.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
