utterances.text: You will agree with me that the total would be about 30 per cent of the incomplete birth-dates?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of that order, between 20 and 40 per cent but I can find the exact figure for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that this is exactly what we can find in your report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you require further information from the witness or not? Because he has offered to look further and give you a more precise answer. So it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have consulted the findings and what the witness has just told us does not differ very much from his written report, and for that reason I don't want to spend any more time on this. I believe that we have agreed that the figure would be around 30 per cent, and I'm happy with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, I just found the figure, 28.8 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have mentioned names, similar names, the same names. As I was perusing your report I could see that you had a lot of problems with the way some people's names on the missing list and in the census are spelt. What was the discrepancy there when you matched the list of missing persons with the census list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was -- the main reason for the discrepancy was that in the census, the names were written down by the enumerators, and later, the forms were scanned and transferred automatically to files. But these names were never corrected because of the war situation. So usually when you do this kind of scanning, you should check. But there was never time to do that according to the statistical, statistics office in Sarajevo. Anyway, it was not high on their agenda and because names are not important for a statistical exercise. You do not need the correct names to makes statistics on the age distribution of a municipality, for example. So when we looked at it, we had to correct, we checked many of the names and we found that some of the names were, the scanning was inaccurate, say that an "LJ" was read by the scanner as "Q", for example, and Q is not a letter that is common in the -- in Bosnian names. So when we discovered that, we made that change. Also, we could look at members' names of a whole family, living together, and say Music was written with "MV" instead of "MU", then we made that change. If the other family members were written "Music", we changed the Mvsic to Music. So that was the main cause of the errors. In the ICRC list of missing persons, the names are written much more correctly, although there were some mistakes there also.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In other words, you had a lot of problems collating the names on the list of missing persons with the census list. In order to complete your task, did you apply different criteria of collating the data in order to be able to identify all these persons?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes we checked just the first three letters of a surname, of a person, to -- because there could be errors in letters number 4 and 5 and 6. And then we did a visual inspection afterwards. So we tried various methods to get around all the mistakes. This comparison was not done for the first version of this report in the year 2000, but later we improved the technology and we did then this match, and we also made a list of correct names which -- from person familiar with name traditions made for us and we compared then all the real, the names reported in the census with the list of correct names. And made corrections with it when necessary or used the correction. We never deleted the name as reported in the census but we tried to find a more correct name or writing of the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that an ideal situation would be when, between the person that you are trying to identify and the person on the census list, everything matches, the name, the family name, the father's name and the date. However, when this is not the case, how many and what criteria did you use in order to be able to match the persons on the missing list and the census?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used a number of different criteria, say only year of birth and first -- and name, because as I said, the exact date of birth was missing for some persons. And we also checked the year of birth plus minus three or four years, to identify possible candidates for matches. Used only the two or three or four first letters. In the ICRC list of missing persons, the father's name was unfortunately -- sorry, it was correct reported. In one of the data sources, the father's name was not reported. But the maticni broj was not reported in the ICRC list so we could not use that for matching. So we used many different criteria and combinations of them to find candidates for matches and checked outwards. But also, there were also a number of cases where there was an exact match, where for date of birth and name and place of birth and everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You will then agree with me that you have used a total of 71 criteria in order to identify a person, at least this is the information that I have.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, up to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Starting with the full name, the initials and so on and so forth. My question now is this: Given all the difficulties that you faced and the criteria you used, was there a percentage within the total number of identified persons for whom you could state that all the data matched to a high degree or maybe 100 per cent and again we are starting with the name, the date of birth, and then all the other data about the person?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We kept logs when we did this matching and certainly we could go back to the logs and see the number -- the proportion that came out with the exact 100 per cent match. That's possible. We did not include all this detail in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In your report, therefore, you did not mention that there was 100 per cent match or 60 per cent match or 50 per cent match, and you have not provided us with the means to check the reliability of the match or alternatively, that the match was only relative to a certain degree?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey? I can anticipate --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Three part, relatively complicated question so if we could break it down I think it would be better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's a good suggestion, which you should take up.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be happy to.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brunborg, I'll try to put it in simpler terms although I think you have understood me. When you did the matching, you had a certain percentage with complete information about a person who is on the missing list and who is also on the census. There is no problem there. After that, you have a person who is on the census and on the missing persons list, you have only a year of birth for them or a name without the last name, or vice versa, only last name, no first name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I think you will agree with me that, say, a spelling mistake with a "Q" instead of an "LJ" is of no significance here and we did not feel a need to report every detail as a -- as I said. And also regarding the date of birth, if it's on one of the lists, it says 1st of November, 1980, and the other one says 2nd of November 1980 or just November 1980, we could almost certainly conclude that this was a correct match. I think the report is difficult enough to read, and perhaps not that interesting, and it's complicated to read and with more detail it would have been unreadable altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can agree with you only in part. My question was not about spelling mistakes, though, or not a mistake in the date of birth by a day. But lack of one part of a name or a lack of year of birth, how could you identify that person with somebody who is on the census?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, date of birth was lacking for just a handful of persons, very few. But even in those cases, we used the other available person, data, names and say place of birth, place of residence and so on. And if it were consistent and there were no other persons with similar information, then we can conclude. Remember that we did not only look at a one-to-one match. We compared.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We also looked at people with similar characteristics, similar names, similar date of birth and so on. One interesting example is a question of twins because twins are born on the same day, have the same father's name, same family name, born in the same place and often have similar first names also so we have to be very careful not to confuse twins as being duplicates, duplicate and wrong -- wrong records, for example. And also, if we match a missing person from the ICRC list with the census and there are -- one of them is a twin, we have to be careful that we are matching with the right twin.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think that must have been an exception, if it occurred at all. I'm interested in the 7.661 persons that you used about 70 criteria to identify. Let me come back to your report of the 16th November 2005. I will call it into e-court so you can look at it. It's 1341. I'm sorry, for some reason it's not in e-court. Could you please look at your report of the 16th November, table number 7, it's on English page 23.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you were compiling this, you were guided by the 1991 census, right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you established the gender and ethnic structure of Srebrenica victims in table 7, as shown here. But the ethnic affiliation of the persons who were not matched is left unknown and that's what we see in column 5, unknown.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but let me add that we did not use only the census 1991 to establish ethnicity but also the PHR list that recorded ethnicity for more than 5.000 so it's a combination but you're correct it was unknown for 13.4 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Is that the 13 per cent that we discussed at the beginning of my cross-examination when you said that in relation to 13 per cent of the population, you were unable to make an identification with the data you had from the 1991 census, or in other words, 87 per cent were identified?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think more or less, but there were of course also some records in this -- in the census where that question was unrecorded. Must have been some, but not a high proportion, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So these 13.4 per cent remained unknown. Could you please look at table 10, which is on page 28 of your report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You broke down dead and missing men for Srebrenica by ethnicity and municipality of residence?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On what basis did you break down the 999 unknown men, for which you had no data on ethnicity or data from the 1991 census who are practically non-existent in 1991?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very simple. We just -- we assumed in this table number 10, that the distribution by ethnicity for the 13 per cent was the same as for the 87 per cent. This is a very common method in demography, a sort of pro-rating or proportionality principle. We did not, of course, assign ethnicity to any individual that we did not know the ethnicity for. This was only done on a group basis for statistical purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We are talking about a total of 1300 out of which 999 are men, speaking of table 10. Using this method of distribution of those 999 persons who do not exist on the list of 1991, to what extent is this affecting other tables with complete data, where you have the gender distribution, ethnic composition, et cetera, of the population?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the gender was known for everybody, from the -- from the -- in the missing lists. We did not need to consult the census to establish the gender. It was only done for ethnicity and also for age distribution. We assumed the same distributions as for those that were known. This is the very same principle that is used when we are doing sample surveys. We assume that the sample, whether it is 5.000 for a big country, is representative of the whole population. And we did not see any reason why there should be a bias here that the ethnic distribution should be different from those without -- that we did not manage to match.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. And you emphasised below table 10 that the numbers are adjusted according to the original distribution of original data. If we had an adjustment in this table, does that mean you also adjusted data in other tables?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In some of the tables. Table 11, I think, and all the figures on page -- and table 9, I think we adjusted there also. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I just want to take you back to your article, speaking of how many people were killed in the genocide. It's in e-court P02420, English version, pages 3 and 4. If you have that article with you, if not, we will try to -- you write, "Fearing --"

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Pages 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: "Fearing what might happen when the VRS occupies the territory" -- I apologise to the interpreters. "When the VRS government takes over the enclave, a group of men numbering perhaps 15.000, mainly of military age, started walking through wooded hills towards the territory controlled by the federal BH army." My question is: Based on what information and what sources did you estimate this number to be 15.000?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was provided to us by the Office of the Prosecutor based on general reports and findings by various organisations. I'm not sure about the source, whether -- probably military, some of the sources. But this is a very rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And it is not based on any exact data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. As you also read, the formulation is "numbering perhaps as many as 15.000". So the inexactness of it is emphasised.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that that column was armed and moved through various places that later became the subject of your research, that armed clashes occurred between that column and the BH army on the one hand and the forces of the VRS, I'll tell you, it was Kamenica, Baljkovica, Buljim?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that that happened, yes. My understanding is that a long column was a mixture of armed people and people who were not armed. And there was regular clashes and there was also shelling, shelling of people who were not armed. So it was a very mixed situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In your studies so far, when you were attempting to establish the structure, the composition, of missing persons, in all your reports so far I have found that you came in every case to the conclusion that they were civilians. Does that mean that using all your sources, you determined that missing persons were exclusively civilians?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not think we wrote that anywhere, that the missing persons were civilians. We had no information about that. We only reported the number of missing persons, whether civilian or not, whether killed in combat or not. We were not tasked to find out, to find out whether they were civilians or not or died in combat or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you note any sources or lists of the BH army at the time when were you doing your studies? Did you consult any lists of fighting men who went missing or were killed in that period?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I did the first study, we had no access to such data but such data has later -- have later become available, on the -- on lists of men who died, soldiers who had died.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And within that number of 7.661 dead and missing persons, did you try to establish, which is important for the Court, how many of them were civilians and how many were military men?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. We were not asked to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So you never ever looked at the lists made by the BH army after year 2000 and which is stored in the demographic section of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: My colleagues looked at this list, of course. I did not personally look at the list. And the data in that list were utilised to estimate the total number of killed persons in the armed conflicts in Bosnia, and also used to check whether there were people who were killed in fighting elsewhere, who might be on the missing lists, for example, on the missing list for Srebrenica, who died elsewhere. Then they should not be reported as missing in connection with the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And are you aware that within 7.661 persons, there were about 3.000 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you were testifying on the 1st of February this year, on page 6807, in response to a question from the Prosecutor, did you establish that any person from that list died before 1995? Your response was that you did not find a single such case. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember his exact wording but we did check and there might have been some examples of that but then they were deleted from the list. They were not included because the date of disappearance or dates of death was very important for defining who should be included in our list or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know, since your successors and your colleagues did deal with the BH army list, do you know that on the official list of the BH army of dead and missing persons, there are about 100 soldiers who died, got killed, before July 1995 and whose personal information coincide almost to 100 per cent with persons who are on your list of 7.661 persons?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have seen claims for that before, and we have checked, and they were not correct. So we would welcome a list on those to check if there were any errors in that, if that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So you are not aware of the information that I've just quoted and that we have at our disposal, that there are 100 soldiers on your list who died before July 1995, with full names and surnames and other data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Has this list been provided to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It will be. Thank you, Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Nikolic. Mr. Ostojic, will you go next? That was the understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, we'll have a break at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Brunborg, good afternoon. We met before, my name is John Ostojic. I represent Beara here. I have a couple questions that I'd like you to help me to understand, so I could understand your report better. So bear with me if I don't get all the terms right, and I'm sure you'll be helpful, as you have been in other cases. Sir, if I may summarise, your report is conducted basically in a three-prong analysis, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say that. Would you like to mention those three prongs, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sure. The way I view it is that you have first what's called informational sources that you gathered as you testified here today, and then you used the methodology, which I think you either called matching or linkage methodology, and then ultimately you have your conclusions, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that basically the sum and substance of your report and analysis?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say that. Then, of course, we look at all the results and check whether they are reasonable or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right. The analysis to reach the conclusion, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now this report was prepared by three specific individuals, yourself and two others. What part of the report did you perform and what part did, for example, Dr. Tabeau and Dr. Hutland [phoen] prepare?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember in detail who wrote what. When you cooperate in scientific analysis, the different parts are often mixed, but I can say that Dr. Tabeau did most of the work on the missing, exhumed missing persons, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, doctor, when I looked at your report I saw some words that I take exception with and that is with all due respect of course to you, sir, that is like the word "killing", and my understanding just recently in your testimony, that you did not do any analysis to determine whether a victim was -- died as a result of being killed or died as a result of other causes, did you?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why would you include it in your report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you find the example, an example, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. How about page 3? Where you talk about what your objective was, to actually to arrive at a reliable estimate of the number of people who were killed or missing, on the bottom of the page, the very last line?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm. Well, that may unfortunately have been a -- have been imprecise. Of course, when people are exhumed from mass graves, it's pretty sure they were killed. Otherwise, it would be more correct in this context to say that they were dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about the word "execution" when you use it in your report is that also inaccurate? Because in fact you didn't conduct any studies or analysis to determine whether any of those individuals or victims who were exhumed met their death by execution. Why would you use that word?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because these people found in mass graves. People found in mass graves were most likely executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, can you point where in your report or any of the versions that you have including the 16th November 2005 report, where you consulted, as a source, any of the anthropological studies that were performed by various doctors or anthropologists working with the Office of the Prosecutor to make that link or connection?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was done -- we did not consult those reports. This was done by the ICMP, and, well, there are other witnesses testify on the cause of death. We are not concerned with the cause of death, just the death itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's what I thought. That's why I found it a little uncomfortable that you as a demographer would have used those terms. Because you're not giving us any opinions here, are you, sir, as to the cause of deaths by any of these victims that you identify or classify as missing or dead?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. The problem is that as a demographer, writing for academic journals and reports, what you write there is slightly different from what you would present in a trial, in that you have to be much more accurate in a trial about the wording than in, say, in a more general article.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So let me understand, doctor, if you will. You did not rely or use any of the OTP sources, such as the anthropologists', the pathologists' or the archeologists' reports in reaching any of your conclusions here; correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only generally. We knew about it, of course, and I've read reports, when the reports on how people were found blindfolded and shot from behind, but we did not link that specifically for each individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the evidence is overwhelming, as I think you will agree, that there were -- there were killings and executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't agree necessarily that it was overwhelming but we won't go into a debate on that, doctor. There were some undoubtedly. You have done no independent research to make any classification of the war-related deaths, have you?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not here, no. If you mean war related if you mean combat, is that what you mean or did do you mean in general war so that natural deaths would not be included or --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll explain it. You'll agree with me don't that you in the field of demography there is this kind of new and emerging area called classification of war-related deaths, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But most of it is concerned with battle-related deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But within that classification, with all due respect, you yourself identify four categories, don't you, battle-related, non-battle-related, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one distinction, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What are the other categories? I mean you wrote the article only a month ago, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, civilian, non-civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you can also talk about direct and indirect causes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And in this emerging new area of demography, your first article that you wrote about these classifications of war-related deaths appeared in 2005 before this report of the 16th of November 2005; correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which article are you referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the article entitled, "Demography of conflict and violence, an emerging field."

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Springer 2005, by yourself as one of the authors and Dr. Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was, I don't think well it was introduction to a special issue of --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: European Journal of Population [speakers overlapping]

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the interpreters ask you to speak a little more slowly and make a pause between questions and answers, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the witness. We have the usual problem. When two persons are speaking the same language, they tend to be very quick on the draw. So please allow a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps you should change language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would be easy for Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I may proceed, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, when we talk about these classifications of war-related deaths, the battlefield or battle-related deaths, how are they defined?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never did that analysis myself. This is done by a research centre in Uppsala in Sweden and Oslo, Norway. And these are people who died in battle, in fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Both military and civilians, meaning soldiers and civilians, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's another distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm looking at your paper again with Dr. Tabeau and Henrik Urdal, where you make the distinction that battlefield deaths, and I think it's on page 7 of your article that you consider battle-related deaths, including soldiers and civilians killed in combat?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The other category is non-battle deaths?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How would you define that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be people who died from, say, disease in -- or lack of medication in a conflict situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Or how about the elderly under stress?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible, you could also call that an indirect cause of a conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Or how about isolated killings from a third party, a neighbour?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's related to the conflict, yes. If it's a regular murder, then it's not. It's often difficult to distinguish these, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, what are the other categories? You mentioned four in your article but I was only able to find two in reading your article, the battle-related and the non-battle-related deaths?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian and non-civilian, so two times two is four.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. You would agree with me that demography is really a science which just produces estimates on whatever it is that you might be analysing such as population migration, or any socioeconomic analysis that may be involved with that, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can also produce exact figures if the data sources are good.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And what constitutes that a data source is good?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the, say, if you're talking about a total population, that the coverage is good, that the recording of what happened is good. There are different criteria for that. I need to go into detail on a certain case; I could talk about deaths in my own country, how it's recorded, but no country in the world has perfect data on everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So that's why when you spoke last time, you discussed margin of error I was a little confused about your answer, and if you could just help me understand, is margin of error the same thing as a confidence level which we talk about in demography and statistics?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, confidence level is a more precise term based on a probability distribution, whereas margin of error is a more loose term.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can you show me where in your report you've identified any either margin of error or confidence level with respect to any of the sources that you utilised in your first step in reaching your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Confidence intervals are usually estimated when you have -- you're operating with a sample of the population. Then you can estimate sampling errors and we did not have a representative sample of the population so that was irrelevant, you could say. But when we talk about the total number of missing persons, then we try to be on the conservative or low side. We try not to include anybody that should not be included. So the margin of error is always positive, not negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But in order for me or anyone else to digest some of your report, do you think it would be reasonable to say that using this source, whichever source you used, it's a primary source, and that this source actually has a strong or better than good amount of reliability because its margin of error is small?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could say that but we cannot estimate the confidence level of margin of errors because you need probability distributions to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why didn't do you any probability distributions on the various sources that you utilised in your first step for preparing this report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then you would need -- is it too fast now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless I hear from the interpreters, I think it's safe to go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll try to break. To estimate confidence levels or -- then you need either repeated samples or a subsample of a population, and that is not always -- it's usually not available. Say of the 1991 census how can we talk about the margin of error? Then to do that you would have needed a post-enumeration survey or some other source to estimate the data quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's take your example, the census, if you will. I think as a demography you'll agree with me that the census in general has some well-known and inherent flaws or deficiencies in it, corrects?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, the census actually doesn't identify an individual if it's a child, but really the way it works is that the census-taker would capture the data from the head of the household or perhaps the only person who was at the household when he tried to obtain that information; correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And one of the flaws of the census is that certain communities or populations may overinflate the number of people that may or may not be a specific community?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may happen, but I think it's a more common problem is that it is underinflated, that people are not found. People are not at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What other flaws or deficiencies have you found with respect to the census in general others than those that we just discussed?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very general flaw is that the age is reported wrongly. There is something called age heaping where there are more people who are 20 or 25 or 30 years old than those who are, say 29 or 31, but in the Bosnian census that is less of a problem since they were asked about the date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, what about flaws or deficiencies in one of the others sources you used, the voter registration? Did you find any flaws or deficiencies there?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yeah. The most obvious flaw with the voters list is that first people below age 18 were not included and people who did not register to vote were not included, so it's just a sample and an unrepresentative sample of the total population.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Voter apathy, in other words?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, or people who were not there, and in fact, we found that this varied with different ethnic groups, the Croats were the most -- least likely to register to vote in 1997, 98 and the Muslims and Serbs much more likely to register to vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What about the flaws or deficiencies in the 1997 and 1998 editions of the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the editions I'm not aware of any particular flaws there. I think the quality of those later editions are probably better than the first data that were collected in July 1995 in Tuzla and elsewhere in a very chaotic situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What about the PHR list of missing persons? Did you note any flaws or deficiencies in that source?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the same as for the ICRC list, say, that the date of birth was not complete for everybody but it was more complete than for the ICRC lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But if you look at each of your sources, and if you're using that to reach a conclusion, can you tell me with respect to each of the sources that you utilised what was the margin of error of the data that you relied on in order to reach your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we -- sorry, I will try to break. I don't think we had the information available to estimate the margin of error. We talk about all the weaknesses of each data source but it's not always possible to say what the margin of errors is. We can say the completeness of date of birth but we do not know for those who have complete birth how many were still correct or incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And let's stay with the topic of these informational sources just for a few minutes, so that I could flush out a couple things. Am I accurate that you used two primary sources and the remaining were considered secondary sources?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of the secondary sources, do you think any of them were reliable enough to be utilised as a primary source?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: A primary source, the topic here is to -- the agenda is to estimate the number of missing and dead persons. And of course, the census cannot before the war cannot be used to do that. Neither can the voters list collected after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's why they're secondary sources, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, will you agree with me that the quality of the primary and/or secondary sources permit us to assess, to an extent, the credibility and reliability or give any value to the conclusions one may have relying on such data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. May I also add that there is a third primary source and that is the lists of exhumed persons from ICMP which is becoming increasingly important as more bodies are exhumed and identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you use that as a secondary source in your report, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a primary source.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even though the interpreters haven't interjected, once more, please slow down. You need to pause, allow a short interval of time. I mean --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not referring only to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's really it's actually my fault. I apologise to the Court and to the doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't want to pinpoint anyone in particular but you need to cooperate a little bit. Thank you, go ahead, Mr. Ostojic. In four minutes' time we will have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, what other sources were available to you and your demographic team at the Office of the Prosecutor while you were conducting these reports that you did not utilise? I think you mentioned a couple today in your testimony but can you list for me other primary or secondary sources that demographers may typically look at in order to evaluate a certain theory they are trying to establish?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: One was referred to previously by Ms. Nikolic, that is the database of dead persons collected by the federation. The lists of dead soldiers that we used only to a limited extent. There is also a database called -- collected by the Muslims Against Genocide which we really did not utilise very much, which would have added, say, a few hundred missing persons. Then there is the large database collected by Mr. Tokaca in Bosnia on the -- I don't remember the exact title of that database. It includes both dead and other persons. And other victims in conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me understand why your office or your department, if you will, the demographic team, why you wouldn't have used the database of dead persons collected by the federation?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was used for comparison to check whether a missing person was dead or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't note that in your report anywhere. Do you have it in your report, do you know?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would need to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. You'll have to opportunity hopefully if the Court permits at the break.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the amount of the dead or the database from the federation of dead persons is? Do you know the amount that they cite as being dead in their database?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was it something like 40.000, of which very few, perhaps less than 100, were related to the fall of Srebrenica, something --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All right. So they had their database covered the entire state. For Srebrenica, it was far less, to the database or the report that you show us of being 7.000 missing or dead, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but this database covered mostly the territory of the federation and not the other entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whenever it's convenient, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how it is that your team decided not to utilise these other sources?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we were asked to establish the number of missing and dead persons, and this -- the sources we used seemed to be the best but as other sources have become available, say, of exhumed persons then we have-- we have used them. For example, if I may mention that the ICMP database, use of that resulted in 103 persons who should be added to the list of missing and dead persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to talk now about methodology so it might be a good time, if the Court wishes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I will try to speak slower so that we could be able to assist everyone in hearing what the good doctor has to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Glad to hear that, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, although before the break I wanted to discuss methodology, before I do that I do have a couple more questions on the informational sources that you utilised in your research and ultimately reaching your conclusions. But even before that, though, when I looked at your report, I saw what you felt was the objective of the report and we touched on it briefly at the beginning of my cross-examination. Can we turn to that third page and can you help me understand it more? It appears, doctor on the very last paragraph of page 3 and follows on page 4. Am I correct based on what you've told us today that, in fact, your objective was not to arrive at an estimate of the number of people who were killed but only as it relates to the number of people who were missing and/or considered dead?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. So I apologise for some unfortunate wording there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's what I understood but I just wanted to make sure I'm clear on that. Now when we discussed briefly the quality of various informational sources, whether they are primary or secondary, would you, as a demographer, ever look at some control features to determine their credibility or reliability, such as synthetic errors, synthetic errors, balancing errors, late adds or whole-person imputations?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Imputation, I would not use in this connection at all because imputation is assigning values for where there are no values so we did not do that at all. What do you mean the other? I was not familiar -- synthetic measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Errors?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Errors I'm not aware what you mean -- what is meant by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about balancing errors?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Balancing? A balancing equation, you mean, for a population, births, deaths, a population; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Those concepts, from my understanding, are used in demography to assess the reliability of a various source that might be utilised in preparing an analysis or reaching a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that case, I think we have -- use it without using that terminology, that we, of course, we evaluated all sources for, to get as strong results as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us or quantify for us, by utilising percentages, the strength of each of the sources that you utilised?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you talk about percentage, you have to say per cent of what, per cent error? Talked about -- we have talked about per cent missing full date of birth. That is one percentage. We could give you a list of missing variables for all the data sources. That is one kind of percentage error.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, for purposes of completeness, if we look at the data and there were missing factors or missing data, I should say, sorry, missing data on various different factors such as, as you say, the months, the year is given and maybe the month wasn't or the day was not, did you ever look at all those different features and say that 15 per cent of this factor was missing, 12 per cent of another factor was missing, such as a father's name, 20 per cent of something else such as a date of birth was missing, and then actually do what statisticians and scientists and demographers do and come up with a net proportional percentage as to what the margin of error is as to the reliability of that primary or secondary source?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did look at all those variables and say how complete is each variable. But again, I don't think the margin of error is a well-defined concept that can be estimated in the way you are suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that in the demographic reports that you've conducted as you list in your curriculum vitae, that in all of those reports, other than the reports relating to a war crimes or battlefield areas, war conflicts, all of them, in fact, have a margin of error?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, yes. No data set is perfect but we usually don't talk about margin of error except for sample surveys where there is well-defined methodology to estimate the sampling variance of the, say of a proportion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you why I ask, because in my view, if you have a poor quality or less than an adequate quality of an individual source or many sources and then you utilise even a poor or less than adequate methodology, that would impact, would it not, sir, on the ultimate conclusions one would reach?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and no. Sometimes you can use statistical methodology that will improve the results. You can use regression methods, even if the data are poor and you can come up with stronger -- strong estimates. So methodology can improve the results.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, perfect kind of entry into the next topic, methodology. How did you and your team determine that the match or linkage methodology was the most appropriate to use in this case or this project that you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we were working on data on individuals, and we have several different data sources that is the only methodology you can use. You have data for the same events from several sources. Say you have ICRC list of missing persons, PHR list of missing persons, several versions of each of these, they are covering the same events with a large degree of overlap, so we need to delete the overlap so we get a unified list, instead of duplicates and overlaps. And also to check with the census, that is the -- this is standard procedure, merging or matching variables is standard in, for demographic analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the word standard but there is things known in methodology as standard and non-standard methodology, is there not?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What would some of those methodological theories be? You listed one or the matching and I think today on page 53, on line 4, you mentioned another one, proportionality principle. What are some of the other standard methodological ways you would utilise in order to assess the sources that you were analysing?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a demographer, it's very natural to use graphs or tables to study the age distribution, for example, age and sex distribution of a population or of the events of a part of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, is that a methodology or is that just a way of doing it so it makes a little more sense to reduce the amount of data that you have in a more simpler form?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that looking at age distribution is a sort of basic demographic methodology. It's not very sophisticated but it's still very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And now, just briefly tell me what your opinion is based upon a reasonable degree of scientific and demographic certainty of the quality of a sample methodology? Is it less precise? Would you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually it is less. A sample is less precise than a full, a data set covering the full population but it depends of course about the quality of the data source covering the full population.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I agree. It always depends on the quality of sources, right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But with respect to sample methodology, would you agree with me that it's the least precise methodology that can be used?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Tell me, if you will, what the flaws of a sample methodology are?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That it is covering only a part of the population, but the basic issue is of course whether the sample is biased or not, whether it's a representative sample. If it is a representative sample, then we can estimate the sampling variance and we can get, if the sample is large enough, we can get fairly good estimates of the issues we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So those two points, bias and representativeness, which one weighs more in determining whether the sample methodology would be considered less precise?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's really the same thing, bias and representativeness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask the speakers to slow down, please? We cannot follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic and witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar, sir, with the methodology known as the lost function analysis?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lost function? Loss -- lost or loss.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Lost?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not lost. But I'm familiar with the loss function analysis. Maybe it refers to the same thing. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Maybe. What is it?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Loss function is can be considered a function trying to evaluate the loss or the disadvantage of a certain issue, I think, say, but it's not so much in demography. Say what would be the loss of not building enough schools in a country.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What about the methodological idea of total error model? Have you heard of that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid not but if I may I'm not a mathematical statistician so there may be many concepts that I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, did you, at any point, sir, try to determine or obtain from the Office of the Prosecutor data from various United Nations sources as to the movement of the population from Srebrenica in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We talked to the -- to people in the OTP about sources on that. I also tried to investigate, myself, on visits to Bosnia, whether there were data, but we did not come across any reliable sources on that, that could be utilised in this, that were really relevant for the issues we looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What quality controls did you put in place to determine or to verify that the methodology that you were utilising was reliable or accurate?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, almost everything that we wrote in the report is about quality control. For example, checking whether the missing persons were actual or fictitious and that they lived in the area where they approximately the same area as they disappeared. That is one kind of quality control. The other and very important quality control was to find out if any of the missing persons were survivors, in fact, whether they registered as displaced persons after the war or whether they registered to vote, because dead and missing people cannot vote. And we did that and we found very few numbers, low numbers, between 10 and 20, and showing that although there might be such cases, it was not a large-scale phenomenon. There was no organised campaign to register people as missing, surviving people. On the other hand, a few people may have registered to vote in the name of a dead or missing person.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Earlier -- thank you. Earlier today, you had mentioned to my learned colleague Mrs. Nikolic, that on page 39, I think line 19 through 22, when she was asking you about the number of people who were actually in Srebrenica before the fall of the enclave, and you, sir, said, and I'll try to quote it you said, "The number of people whether it was 20.000 or 40.000 is not really, as far as I can see, very significant, when we discuss the number of people who are missing or dead after the fall of Srebrenica, because we have that list of people." I'm just giving that to you as a context. My question is you said it is not, as far as you can see, not very significant. Does that mean that it is significant or it's not significant at all to you?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context, it is not significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, don't you agree with me that as a further quality control on the data, whether it's the sources and the quality of the methodology you used, that it's important as a demographer to have an understanding specifically of how many people were in the Srebrenica enclave before July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in general, yes. We knew that there were large numbers. We heard from UNHCR and other sources but what we really would have wanted and which I tried to get was a list of people who were in the enclave, a list with names and date of birth and so on. That would have been very useful but we did not locate any such list and I doubt that if it exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it was my understanding from your testimony that you felt that the 40.000 figure may have been somewhat inflated, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people claimed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. What do you claim?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that, since there are no reliable source, as far as I know, to the exact number of people, we know the population of Srebrenica in 1991, as it was enumerated but since 1991 there were many flows in many different directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The demographic team that you had to what extent did you evaluate those various flows from 1991 through 1995 to be able to assess what the population was?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not evaluate those flows. We learned about them. We read about them. But since there were no good estimates we were not concerned about those flows and the number of people in Srebrenica in 1995, only with the number who were -- went missing in 1995, after the fall of the enclave. So whether half of the population went missing or one-third or one-quarter, or 100 per cent, is not really interesting here, as far as I can see. It's only -- we are talking about the total number of people who went missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Respectfully, I disagree with you. As a further quality control, did you look at the reports by the various pathologists, anthropologists and archeologists to determine whether -- the extent of the exhumations did they exhume how many graves, primary or secondary, do you have that information?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had a look at it but particularly the ICMP data which is now based more and more on DNA analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We will get to the ICMP data but I'm asking about the various pathologists, et cetera, that worked in the same office you did at the Office of the Prosecutor. Were you able to obtain their information to determine the number of exhumations they conducted and the number of mass graves they may have uncovered?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did get that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And as you sit here, do you know how many mass graves were exhumed?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall now but when I wrote the first report in -- which was published in the year 2000, there had been 1900 exhumations, I think, bodies that had been exhumed. And 70 had been identified, something like that. That was the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it's reflected in your report in 2005 as well, specifically that. My question is do you know how many mass graves there were?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall, because it's changing all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many -- from those mass graves, how many were exhumed?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall but on the other hand, I don't see how that is really relevant for the estimate of the total number of missing and dead people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, doctor, I think it goes to quality control. Do you know what the conclusion was of the pathologists, anthropologists and archeologists as to the number of bodies that were actually exhumed from the mass graves?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I've read many reports but we are trying to quantify for each individual and they were not at that time, there were not enough reports on identified individuals. But now with the ICMP, we have a large number of reports. But as I said before, whether anthropologists or pathologists decide that this person had been shot or not, was of no significance for our work since we are not concerned about the cause of death but only the death itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it would be in your opinion as you sit here today the responsibility or the job duty of the pathologists, to render a decision as to what was the cause of death, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let me show you 2D0003. You'll have it available on your screen, I think, in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think it's already in evidence, Your Honour, so you should have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, just looking at the top portion of this, as a scientific demographer, you can obviously see and I'll walk you through it, it's a report dated the 19th of July 1995, and it seems to be from a United Nations organisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it seems to be going to the head of the United Nations at the time in New York, in America, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If this is a report prepared by the United Nations for the United Nations, would you consider this, sir, based upon a reasonable degree of certainty, as being a reliable primary source?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- we would have to consider it more to see how reliable it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, we will do that but share with me, if you will, the factors that you would utilise in determining whether a source is reliable or not.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Especially where the data came from, and how the data were collected and evaluated and analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if the Office of the Prosecutor ever showed you this report or outgoing cable, as it's called?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think he can see all of it. If we are going to ask questions on the complete report or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Mr. McCloskey is perfectly right, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't have objection to that at all, Your Honour. I can tender him a clean copy if you'd like, if the Court permits or wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree to that, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, could you assist?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I recognise it's in e-court I thought maybe for his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In e-court you only get one page at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's what I thought. I agree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted initially to know the factors that you consider relevant in determining whether a source such as this would be considered reliable.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reasonably reliable, I assume, but it doesn't -- it says, for example, "6.600 DPs are accommodated by UNPROFOR at the Tuzla air base" - there is no information here about how they collected that information but it's probably reasonably reliable - "but the other 17.000 DPs are currently unaccounted for. In 1993 UNPROFOR estimate the population of Srebrenica to be 42.000." It doesn't say anything about how they arrived at that estimate so we -- really, I cannot conclude anything about the quality of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, doctor, were you ever shown this document during the time that you were preparing your reports with respect to the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall but it's not impossible that I've seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, as a demographer, when you see something like this, as you just stated, it would be curious to find out the basis of their conclusion and to determine whether it was reliable, would it not?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What efforts, if any, did you or your staff conduct to determine the reliability of the data that's provided on this exhibit, 2D0003?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard about these estimates, here, about 42.000 in Srebrenica, and we did try to locate lists or -- and more evidence on that. Asking both the OTP and in Bosnia and elsewhere but we did not come up with anything. So since our work was based on data on individuals only, this was not of great help to us, saying 42.000 population, and that was in 1993. It doesn't say anything about 2005, I believe, glancing at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Really, doctor, we are not -- I appreciate I think you mean 1995, right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, 1995.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "1993 population of Srebrenica to be 42.000". That was three years before the events we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Two, but with the margin of error that's close enough. Did you do any research or conduct any studies to determine what the population in either 1993, 1994 or 1995 in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, we investigated whether there were databases or lists, handwritten or electronic or anything available, but we did not obtain anything because without names, we could not -- this wouldn't be of any value to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you contact the United Nations to determine if they had any of that data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were working at the United Nations. And OTP is part of the United Nations. We, I think we did ask UNHCR, which is also part of the United Nations, whether they knew about lists. I talked to the mayor of Srebrenica, and asked whether they knew about such lists, and some people said they had heard about such lists but nobody knew for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the MUP to determine whether or not those lists are in existence?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did visit MUP both in Tuzla and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what information, having visited that place, those places, would you have gathered or were you anticipating on obtaining?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP had a register of -- and we did get some lists from the MUP. But in this difficult and chaotic situation, the MUP could not possibly register all the movements of people into and out of Srebrenica. Moreover, we could only meet with the MUP of the federation, not of the Republika Srpska, which was covering Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, doctor, why, on the second page of this document, in the -- right above the number 5, if you know, the reference that these are imprecise figures? Do you see it? "Due to the imprecise nature of these figures," do you see that line?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It goes on to say, "We recommend that any public statements are limited to the broad reference of several thousand missing." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were you ever told that, that it should limit any public statements to a broad reference?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but, sir, this is dated July 19, two weeks or one week, less than one week after the events, where the full scale of the events were not known. Since then, ICRC and PHR collected lists of missing persons and so one year later, much more information was known, much more was known about the situation. At that time, I totally agree, too little was known to say anything more accurate than several thousand missing but much more became known in the next half year or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But in fact the figures that they cite specifically with the people that made it to, as it's called, the free territory from Srebrenica, they are very specific, are they not, on the first page, third paragraph, I believe? They even give the specific town and the specific number of people that are a--

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our main interest in those who arrive but in those who did not arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But the data that they have with respect to those that arrived, do you know if your demographic team ever evaluated that data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No we did not because these are only aggregate figures, no individual data here, and they do not tell about the number of victims, only about the survivors.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you really believe that the numbers on paragraph number 2, sir, are aggregate figures as opposed to precise figures?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aggregate means collective, so of course they are aggregate. There is no lists, maybe such lists exist, of how many, say, Tuzla town, 500, but how could we have used those even if we had lists? We could not have used them really to collate for estimating number of missing persons or for quality control.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: See, I suggest that you can use that list as quality control because if there is a list of the people that were there, not knowing the number of people who were in the actual enclave, you could determine whether or not those people appear on your missing list. And that in fact it would be although you're not a mathematician, a cross check if you will of the data and information that you're supplying, which would render it more reliable than less reliable, wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what we did. With all the lists that became available to us, we did a cross check to see whether there were survivors. We are talking about whether there were survivors among the missing, as reported, as registered in Tuzla and elsewhere. And whenever we used the number of such lists to do that, exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I may have misunderstood your previous answer, then. Did you utilise the data that's reflected on this joint crisis action team and specifically from the BiH local authorities, in order to prepare your report dated the 16th of November 2005?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not directly at that time, but we did later obtain the database on displaced persons, which should then include those 18.333 DPs, et cetera, and all the other numbers so they were collected and put together in a systematic fashion later on we did check whether there were missing persons on the -- in the displaced persons database.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I apologise, maybe I'm just not understanding you. I'll give it one more try with the Court's indulgence, if permitted. What I'm suggesting to you, sir, is you should have looked at the data with the names of the specific survivors that were collected by the BiH authorities as well as this JCAT in order to determine whether or not there was any duplication from the list of actual confirmed survivors to the list that you have of missing.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes but we did not obtain such lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What efforts did you take, undertake, to obtain those lists?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked to a number of institutions, United Nations, international, and national institutions, to get lists of both victims and survivors.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And no one to this date, sir, has given you this JCAT report or the BiH authorities data reflecting the information that's prepared here for the United Nations in New York, correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but again, if I also may repeat myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, meaning I'm right, or no they have provided?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: They have not provided. But we did get the list, database on displaced persons later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you can just turn quickly to page 12 of your report, I have just a couple questions to clarify and better understand your report.
